title: A friend's question
hookLine: on the Emmaus road the risen Jesus asks 'What things?' and lets two sad friends tell it all
tomorrow: why do the Buddha's teachings open with 'Thus have I heard'?

lines: TWO SAD FRIENDS ON THE ROAD.
IT HAPPENED TO HIM. WHY ASK?
cards: Can I ask you something kind of personal? The text lands, and before the question even arrives, you're drafting the answer. Luke's Gospel has a stranger who does the opposite.
On the same day the tomb is found empty, two followers of Jesus are walking to a village called Emmaus, talking it over, sad. A stranger falls in beside them.
Luke tells us it's Jesus, risen, but their eyes are held so they don't know him. He asks what they're discussing. One of them, Cleopas, says: are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who hasn't heard?
And Jesus says: "What things?" It happened to him. So why ask?

teach.h: HE LETS THEM TELL IT ALL.
teach.b: Because he lets them tell it. All of it: the prophet they followed, the cross, the hope they'd had. "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel."
The women at the empty tomb, the confusion.
Only when they've told the whole story does he speak, opening the scriptures to them as they walk. At the village he makes as if to go on, and they ask him to stay.
At the table he breaks the bread, and they know him, and he's gone. Then they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?"

teach.h: KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.
teach.b: In Luke's story, the risen Christ walks beside people on the road, and is known in the breaking of bread, the same thing he did with bread at the Last Supper. And notice the order.
Question first. Listening second. Speaking third.
So when a friend asks what you believe, the story's answer is a question back: what things? What's behind the question? Let them tell it all before you say much at all.

how: Christians read the Emmaus road (Luke 24) as Christ walking alongside people and being known in the breaking of bread; people who borrow it answer a friend's question by asking and listening first.

o: a question from a friend, met by listening first
a test a friend sets to see what you'll say
a question you answer fast so it isn't awkward

games.q: the road to Emmaus: tap the pairs.
p: the only stranger who hasn't heard?

s: in Luke, the two travelers recognize Jesus right away
their eyes were held; they knew him at the breaking of bread.
Jesus asks them what happened, though it happened to him
listening first means never saying what you think
the overcorrection. on the road he listens, then opens the scriptures and talks with them.

games.q: your aunt, recently widowed, says over lunch, 'i don't know what i believe anymore.' you have a lot of thoughts. what fits the Emmaus road?
o: ask what's been happening, and let her tell it all before you say much.
share the most comforting belief you know right away, so she isn't stuck.
change the subject gently; big questions at lunch only make it harder.
games.why: on the road, the stranger asks 'What things?' and lets two grieving friends tell the whole story. he speaks only after.

practice: For this sit, just listen. Pick one sound around you, a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breath, and follow it all the way to its end before you name it. When your mind starts drafting a reply to something, come back to listening.

wordCard.voice: A friend's question: a door someone opens to you, met on the Emmaus road with a question back, and a long listen.

orig.note: Greek: what things? Jesus's question to the two travelers on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:19).

carryVoice: Pocket this: listen first, the way the stranger on the road asked, What things? Talk soon.
